name: GPT-4
strengths: Literal, dependable instruction follower — did what you asked and no more
Held a consistent persona and thread across a long conversation, which earlier models lost within a few turns
Broad enough general knowledge to be a default assistant for almost any subject
weaknesses: Answers in one pass — no deliberation, so hard problems fail instantly and confidently
Fabricates citations, APIs and quotes with no signal that it is guessing
Slow token-by-token output that felt sluggish even at the time
notes: The model that defined the 2023 frontier.

name: GPT-4 Turbo
strengths: Noticeably quicker to respond than GPT-4 while keeping most of its judgment
First OpenAI model that could hold a whole document or small codebase in view at once
Reads screenshots, charts and scanned pages well enough to skip a separate OCR step
weaknesses: Truncates long code with placeholder comments instead of finishing the work — the 'lazy model' complaints
Recall thins out toward the middle of a long prompt, so the bigger window isn't fully usable
No way to make it think harder on a question it gets wrong
notes: Announced at OpenAI's first DevDay.

name: GPT-4o
strengths: Conversational latency low enough for real-time voice — it can be interrupted and talk back
Reads images, handwriting and screen captures directly rather than through a caption model
Warm, chatty register that a lot of users still preferred to every model that replaced it
weaknesses: Agreeable to a fault — follows a user's wrong premise rather than correcting it
Answers immediately, so multi-step problems fail in ways it has no chance to catch
Shallow on anything needing a sustained derivation
notes: OpenAI's first natively multimodal flagship.

name: o1
strengths: First model that would genuinely stop and work a problem through before answering
Catches and reverses its own wrong turns mid-reasoning instead of committing to the first path
Best on problems with a checkable answer — proofs, puzzles, tight logic
weaknesses: Long, unpredictable wait before the first token; unusable anywhere interactive
Overthinks trivial questions, spending minutes on what a small model answers instantly
Reasoning is hidden, so you cannot see where it went wrong or steer it
notes: Full release of the o1 series (previewed September 2024).

name: GPT-4.1
strengths: Instruction adherence is the whole point — it honours format rules and negative constraints literally
Predictable latency and behavior, which made it the safe choice for high-volume pipelines
Emits targeted diffs rather than rewriting whole files
weaknesses: Literal to a fault: needs spelling out where a reasoning model would infer intent
No thinking mode, so genuinely hard problems stay out of reach at any prompt length
Long-context recall degrades well before the window's nominal limit
notes: Workhorse non-reasoning line before GPT-5 unified the stack.

name: o3
strengths: Thinks with tools in the loop — searches, runs code, then reasons over what came back
Stays with a hard problem across many steps instead of settling early
Reasoning effort is tunable, so one model covers quick and deep work
weaknesses: Invents confident specifics about its own actions, including claiming it ran code it never ran
Latency swings wildly with effort — the same prompt takes seconds or minutes
Clipped, telegraphic prose that reads as brusque after the 4o line
notes: Pricing reflects the June 2025 cut from $10/$40. OpenAI is retiring o3 from ChatGPT on 2026-08-26 following a 90-day sunset notice; marked deprecated ahead of that date. API availability after the ChatGPT retirement was not specified in the announcement.

name: GPT-5
strengths: Decides for itself when a question deserves deliberation, so you don't pick a model per task
Much readier to say it doesn't know instead of inventing an answer
Holds up better across long multi-file coding sessions than any earlier OpenAI model
weaknesses: Routing misjudgments made quality feel random — the same prompt could get a shallow or a deep answer
Flatter, more clinical voice; users described losing a companion, not just a tool
Under-answers by default, giving a summary where the previous line elaborated
notes: Scores shown for GPT-5 (thinking, high).

name: GPT-5.1
strengths: Spends thinking time in proportion to difficulty, so easy turns come back fast
Warmer and more conversational than GPT-5 without sliding back into flattery
Holds an instruction across a long session instead of drifting back to its defaults
weaknesses: Still misjudges ambiguous prompts, occasionally answering a hard question from the fast path
The gains are in feel and pacing rather than capability — easier to work with, not smarter
notes: Shipped as Instant and Thinking variants.

name: Claude 3 Opus
strengths: Prose quality still cited as a high-water mark — varied rhythm, few assistant tics
Reads subtext, tone and intent where its contemporaries flattened everything
Keeps a long document genuinely in view and answers across it without losing the thread
weaknesses: Slow enough that even trivial requests felt deliberate
Over-cautious — hedges or refuses on benign medical, legal and safety-adjacent questions
One-pass answers, so hard maths and logic fail with no recovery
notes: Flagship of the Claude 3 generation.

name: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
strengths: Wrote code that ran on the first try often enough to change how people used LLMs
Picks up a repo's existing conventions and matches them instead of imposing its own
Fast enough to sit inside a tight edit-run-fix loop
weaknesses: Cuts long files off mid-function, forcing continuation prompts
Adds unrequested scaffolding — comments, validation, try/except you didn't ask for
Single-pass reasoning shows immediately on maths and novel puzzles
notes: Scores reflect the upgraded October 2024 snapshot.

name: Claude 3.7 Sonnet
strengths: You choose per request whether it answers instantly or thinks first — same model, two modes
Thinking is visible, so a wrong assumption can be caught before it acts on it
Carries a plan across many tool calls instead of restarting its reasoning each turn
weaknesses: Over-eager: widens scope, refactors files you didn't mention, edits tests until they pass
Quality tracks the thinking budget, so a small budget quietly gives you a worse model
notes: GPQA/SWE-bench figures use extended thinking.

name: Claude Opus 4
strengths: Runs for hours on one task without losing the thread or looping
Writes notes to itself and picks work back up across sessions
Stops and asks when a requirement is ambiguous rather than guessing
weaknesses: Slow and deliberate — a poor fit for anything interactive
Safety classifiers add refusals and latency to security and biology work
notes: Released with Claude Sonnet 4 at the first Code with Claude conference.

name: Claude Sonnet 4
strengths: Fast enough to live inside an editor loop while still handling multi-file changes
Low-drama behavior — rarely over-reaches or rewrites what you didn't ask about
The default that most people never found a reason to upgrade from
weaknesses: Loses coherence on runs measured in hours where the flagship holds
Settles for a plausible answer sooner on genuinely hard problems

name: Claude Opus 4.1
strengths: Holds several files in mind at once, so a refactor stays consistent across all of them
Fewer collateral regressions — less likely to break something adjacent while fixing a bug
Behaviourally a drop-in: existing prompts kept working unchanged
weaknesses: Feels like the same model with sharper edges rather than a new one
Same slow, deliberate pacing as Opus 4

name: Claude Sonnet 4.5
strengths: Sustains day-long autonomous runs without drifting off the original goal
Drives a real desktop — clicks, scrolls and reads the screen — reliably enough to trust with a workflow
Manages its own context, summarising and discarding what it no longer needs
weaknesses: Hits a ceiling on genuinely novel reasoning; more thinking doesn't produce a better answer
Declares a task finished before verifying that it is

name: Claude Haiku 4.5
strengths: Fast enough for autocomplete, classification and anything where latency is the product
Small, but can still think before answering — unusual at this size
Cheap enough to run many copies in parallel as sub-agents under a larger model
weaknesses: Loses the thread on long tasks; needs a bigger model to plan for it and check it
Takes instructions literally and misses implied requirements
notes: Anthropic's current small model.

name: Claude Opus 4.5
strengths: Effort is a dial, so the same model does cheap quick work and slow deep work
Unusually good at reading a large unfamiliar codebase before it changes anything
Generalises to puzzle types it has plainly never seen rather than pattern-matching
weaknesses: Context felt tight for whole-repository work by the standards of its own moment
Verbose by default — explains its reasoning even when you only wanted the answer

name: Gemini 1.5 Pro
strengths: Genuinely uses its context — finds a single line in a book-length prompt
Watches video and listens to audio natively instead of working from transcripts
Quality holds at input lengths where rivals degraded badly
weaknesses: Mid-pack analysis — the long context couldn't make up for shallow reasoning
Safety filters fired often on plainly benign prompts
Very slow to first token on large prompts

name: Gemini 2.0 Flash
strengths: Fast enough to feel instant inside a user-facing product
Calls tools and generates images natively rather than through a separate pipeline
Cheap enough to run across an entire corpus instead of a sample
weaknesses: Falls apart on multi-step reasoning — fine for extraction, not for analysis
Follows complex formatting instructions unreliably
notes: Included as the price-performance outlier of its generation. SWE-bench Verified 51.8 is Google-reported using an agentic code-execution harness.

name: Gemini 2.5 Pro
strengths: Thinks by default, so you get deliberation without asking or configuring for it
Takes text, images, audio and video in one prompt with no preprocessing
Long context that holds up for whole-codebase and whole-corpus questions
weaknesses: Drops parts of multi-part instructions, especially formatting and negative constraints
Drifts in agentic work — makes edits beyond what was asked
Thinking is hard to bound; it over-deliberates on small requests

name: Gemini 3 Pro
strengths: Strong on abstract, unfamiliar problems rather than remembered ones
Terse and direct by default — it answers instead of performing
Deep Think mode for the rare problem worth minutes of compute
weaknesses: The terseness reads as cold and needs explicit prompting to open up
Old prompt-engineering habits — elaborate personas, hand-written chain-of-thought — make it worse, not better
Deep Think sits behind the top consumer tier rather than the API

name: Llama 3.1 405B
strengths: Runs entirely on your own hardware with no vendor in the loop
Fine-tunes cleanly — the base most of the open ecosystem was built on
Solid across major European languages rather than English with translations bolted on
weaknesses: Needs a multi-GPU node to serve; not a single-machine model
Text-only, so no screenshots, charts or documents
One-pass answers with no way to make it think longer
notes: Pricing shown is typical hosted-inference cost.

name: Llama 4 Maverick
strengths: Sparse routing keeps per-token inference cheap for a model of its size
Accepts images natively, unlike the Llama 3 line
Broad hosting support from day one
weaknesses: Day-to-day quality fell short of the launch impression, and trust never fully recovered
Weak at code and maths against open models released within months of it
Long-context quality degrades well before the advertised limit
notes: Meta's last major open release before its superintelligence-lab reorg.

name: Grok 3
strengths: Pulls live posts and breaking events into answers instead of relying on training data alone
Blunt, unhedged register — it commits to an answer where others disclaim
Reasoning mode available on demand for maths and puzzles
weaknesses: Confident on live-data questions even when the underlying posts are wrong
Uneven at code compared with its maths
Reachable only through the X subscription tiers at launch
notes: Reasoning-mode (beta) scores shown.

name: Grok 4
strengths: Uses tools inside its reasoning rather than after it
A heavy mode runs several attempts in parallel and picks the best for the hardest problems
Genuinely strong on unfamiliar problems that can't be recalled
weaknesses: Very slow to first token because reasoning is always on
Verbose reasoning that inflates cost on work that didn't need it
Its behavior, not its capability, was the story at launch

name: Grok 4.1
strengths: Noticeably fewer fabricated facts than Grok 4 in ordinary use
Better emotional register and creative prose than its predecessor
Still answers directly where rivals hedge
weaknesses: Little published detail on how it behaves at long context or under load
Its real-time-data strengths don't transfer to careful analytical work

name: Mistral Large 2
strengths: French, German, Spanish and Italian treated as first-class languages, not translations
Dense architecture means predictable latency and memory — easy to capacity-plan
Concise by default; it doesn't pad answers
weaknesses: Weights are downloadable but not usable commercially without a licence
Falls behind quickly once a task needs several reasoning steps

name: Mistral Medium 3
strengths: Deploys inside your own VPC or on-premises, which is the entire point for regulated buyers
Consistent, unfussy output for summarising, drafting and translation
Low latency for its capability class
weaknesses: Closed weights broke the expectation Mistral's open releases had set
No deliberation mode, so hard reasoning is simply out of scope

name: DeepSeek-V3
strengths: Sparse routing makes a very large model cheap to run per token
Fully downloadable, so it can go where no external API is permitted
Strong at code and maths relative to what it costs to serve
weaknesses: Text-only — no images, charts or documents
English prose reads stilted and repetitive next to US flagships
Deflects or refuses on politically sensitive subjects

name: DeepSeek-R1
strengths: Shows its full reasoning trace — the model a lot of people learned reasoning from
Open weights meant anyone could distil it into smaller reasoning models
Genuinely strong maths and logic without a frontier lab's budget behind it
weaknesses: Reasoning runs long and repetitive, inflating both latency and cost
Self-censors mid-answer on China-sensitive subjects
Instruction-following and formatting lag well behind its raw reasoning
notes: The 'DeepSeek moment' of January 2025.

name: DeepSeek-V3.2
strengths: Sparse attention keeps long-context work cheap instead of scaling quadratically
Cheap enough to leave running on background reasoning work
Open weights under an unrestrictive licence
weaknesses: An experimental release — behavior shifted noticeably between checkpoints
Prose and instruction-following still trail its reasoning
notes: Listed as V3.2-Exp at release.

name: Qwen3-235B-A22B
strengths: Switches between instant answers and extended thinking inside one model
Very broad language coverage, including low-resource languages most models drop
Permissive licence with no regional restrictions
weaknesses: Loses coherence on long agentic runs where closed models hold together
Thinking mode is verbose and hard to bound
notes: Scores for the July 2025 updated (2507) checkpoints where applicable.

name: Qwen3-Max
strengths: Reliable multi-step tool calling — well-formed calls with correct arguments
Fast for its size thanks to sparse activation
Chinese and English both first-class rather than one as an afterthought
weaknesses: Closed weights, unlike the rest of the Qwen line
Long agentic sessions get verbose, and the verbosity is where the cost goes

name: Kimi K2
strengths: Built to call tools rather than to chat — clean calls, sensible arguments, few loops
A distinct writing voice that avoids the flat assistant register
Answers immediately, with no reasoning wait
weaknesses: No deliberation at all, so hard maths and multi-step logic fail outright
Large enough that self-hosting is a serious infrastructure commitment

name: Kimi K2 Thinking
strengths: Chains hundreds of tool calls without losing the goal — rare stamina for an open model
Research-style depth close to closed models of its moment
Weights available, so the entire agent loop can run in-house
weaknesses: Slow, and it deliberates on nearly everything whether or not it needs to
Needs low-precision serving to be practical, which is fiddly to set up correctly
notes: The strongest open reasoning model as of late 2025.

name: Kimi K3
strengths: Agentic browsing and long-horizon coding are where it feels genuinely frontier-class
Native tool-calling conventions that drop into existing agent stacks without adapters
Reads images and long documents natively, unlike earlier Kimi releases
weaknesses: Slow and very verbose — every request goes through a reasoning pass with no way to switch it off
The effort dial shipped locked at maximum, so cheap quick calls aren't possible
Factual reliability went backwards: it states wrong answers more confidently than K2 did
notes: MMLU-Pro, AIME 2025, and SWE-bench Verified are unconfirmed or conflicting in third-party coverage (AIME cited as both 88% and 96.1%) so left null; Moonshot's own suite reports Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 88.3 and SWE Marathon at 42.0 instead. HLE is 43.5% no tools / 56.0% with tools. Artificial Analysis ranks K3 #3 on its Intelligence Index at 57, with GDPval-AA v2 Elo 1668 (K2.6: 1190), AA-Omniscience +18 on 46% accuracy, and $0.94 per index task at $3.00/$15.00 per MTok — but its hallucination rate regressed to 51% from K2.6's 39%; none of these map to a tracked benchmark key. Weights landed on 2026-07-26 — 96 safetensors shards totalling roughly 1.56 TB, native MXFP4 with MXFP8 activations — under a bespoke Kimi K3 License that attaches conditions to large model-as-a-service and very large commercial deployments, rather than the MIT terms earlier Kimi releases carried.

name: Mistral Large 3
strengths: A fast, broad-coverage generalist tuned for throughput rather than depth
Good backbone for multilingual retrieval over long documents and messy PDFs
Apache-licensed, so it can be self-hosted anywhere without negotiation
weaknesses: Pattern-matches rather than reasons — it doesn't improve if you let it think longer
Context feels short for the long-document work it is otherwise best at
notes: Official pricing $0.50/$1.50; some trackers list hosted rates of $2/$6. GPQA Diamond 67.17 per Mistral's HF model card; not a dedicated reasoning model, so most 2026 reasoning benchmarks are unreported.

name: Gemini 3.1 Pro
strengths: Strong on genuinely novel problems rather than recalled ones
Coordinates several tools in one turn without losing track of which returned what
Direct and efficient by default — no preamble, no filler
weaknesses: Wants the question placed after the data in long prompts, or it under-uses the context
Elaborate prompt scaffolding backfires — it over-analyses the prompt itself
Creative prose is competent but flat
notes: Preview Feb 11, 2026; ARC-AGI-2 reported as 77.1 (76.5 in some sources). Knowledge cutoff Jan 2025 per DeepMind model page. AIME 98.1 is vals.ai-measured (third-party); MMLU-Pro not publicly reported.

name: Qwen3.5
strengths: Very few active parameters per token, so it serves cheaply for its capability
Open weights that fine-tune well and run on commodity inference stacks
Strong multilingual coverage carried over from the Qwen line
weaknesses: Text-only, so it can't take screenshots, diagrams or PDFs
No first-party API — behavior and speed depend entirely on which host you pick
notes: Figures are for the Qwen3.5-397B-A17B open release. MMLU-Pro 87.8 / GPQA 88.4 / SWE-bench 76.4 third-party (LLM-Stats/DeepInfra). Pricing is the DeepInfra hosted FP8 rate — no first-party API for the open weights.

name: Mistral Small 4
strengths: One small model covers reasoning, vision and coding instead of three separate ones
Fits on a single GPU under a permissive licence
Reasoning can be switched off entirely for latency-sensitive work
weaknesses: A fast generalist with a real depth ceiling — it won't reason its way out of a hard problem
Merging three previous lines means it is rarely the best at any one of them
notes: 256k context and $0.15/$0.60 pricing per Mistral's announcement (earlier trackers listed 128k). MMLU-Pro 78.0 / GPQA 71.2 third-party-reported; LMArena Elo 1358 via BenchLM's Arena tracking.

name: Muse Spark
strengths: Health and medical reasoning is its clear specialism, not a side capability
Free inside Meta's consumer apps, so its real user base dwarfs its developer footprint
Deliberate 'contemplating' mode for questions worth extra time
weaknesses: Weak on abstract novel reasoning relative to how strong it is on domain knowledge
No public API at launch — usable only through Meta's own products
notes: Replaced Llama as Meta's flagship line. Closed hosted model — no public API pricing or max-output figure. SWE-bench 77.4 lab-reported; HLE 58.4 is third-party (LLM-Stats), with tools in Contemplating mode; ARC-AGI-2 42.5 in Contemplating mode.

name: GPT-5.5
strengths: Tenacious on long agentic runs — keeps pushing rather than declaring premature victory
Reliably pulls the one relevant detail out of a very long prompt
Deliberately built for agent workloads rather than for chat
weaknesses: Chat quality regressed — shorter, flatter answers and more refusals than the 5.1 line
Struggles to recover once a long thread already contains a wrong assumption
Training artefacts surfaced in production, including a tic for inserting creature words that OpenAI later patched out
notes: GPT-5.5 Pro variant ($30/$180) sits #2 on LMArena. Context reported as 1M API / 1.1M by some trackers. Knowledge cutoff Dec 2025. SWE-bench Verified 88.7 lab-reported; LMArena Elo 1481 is the GPT-5.5 (high) listing.

name: DeepSeek-V4
strengths: Cheap enough to change what you are willing to spend tokens on at all
Whole codebases fit in context, so cross-file work needs no chunking
The small variant is fast and good enough for most work; the large one is there when it isn't
weaknesses: Reads as benchmark-tuned — stronger on tests than in day-to-day use
Serving capacity is chip-constrained, so the top variant is frequently unavailable
No dedicated reasoning line to escalate to
notes: V4-Pro is a 1.6T/49B-active MoE; V4-Flash costs $0.14/$0.28. MMLU-Pro 87.5 / GPQA 90.1 are DeepSeek-reported for V4-Pro in Max reasoning mode; HLE 48.2 is third-party (LLM-Stats), same mode.

name: Grok 4.3
strengths: Very high output throughput once it starts — fast for a model that always reasons
Takes video files directly, with no frame extraction or transcription step
Reasoning is always on, so there is no mode to pick and get wrong
weaknesses: Long wait before the first token, because it always thinks first
Still states wrong facts confidently enough to need grounding for factual work
notes: Requests above 200K tokens are billed at 2x. GPQA Diamond 90.1 per Artificial Analysis (third-party). xAI documents no fixed max-output cap; xAI published agentic (tau2-Bench, IFBench) rather than academic benchmarks at launch.

name: Gemini 3.5 Flash
strengths: The fastest capable option of its moment — iteration speed beats waiting for a better answer
Near-Pro coding quality at Flash latency
Reasoning context carries across turns, so multi-turn agent loops don't re-derive everything
weaknesses: Instruction-following is its weakest axis; tightly constrained output formats slip
Output cap low enough to truncate large generated files
Default effort level shifted at launch, quietly changing behavior for existing prompts
notes: Announced at Google I/O 2026; Terminal-Bench 2.1 76.2%. HLE 40.2 and ARC-AGI-2 72.1 are Google's own figures on the official Gemini 3.5 Flash model card (verified 2026-07-29). SWE-bench Verified 81.0 came from I/O reporting and is NOT on that model card, which reports SWE-Bench Pro (Public) 55.1% instead — treat 81.0 as unconfirmed. LMArena Elo 1481 at launch window.

name: Qwen3.8 Max
strengths: Takes text, images, video and documents in one system — the first Qwen flagship to do all four
Available same-day inside Alibaba's own coding and agent platforms
weaknesses: A preview described as continuously evolving — behavior is a moving target, not a fixed release
No model card or active-parameter count published, so its real speed and cost profile are unknown
Reachable only through subscription plans rather than a per-token endpoint
notes: Announced 2026-07-19 at WAIC Shanghai as a preview, then given a general-availability launch with standard API pricing on 2026-08-03 (Alibaba Cloud Model Studio blog: "Qwen3.8-Max: A New Bar for Coding and Cowork"). Alibaba's own release benchmark table (self-reported, published as an image and not independently re-derivable) claims GPQA Diamond 92.6, Terminal-Bench 2.1 86.6, HLE 43.6, and SWE-bench Pro 67.7 (not the SWE-bench Verified variant this site tracks, so left unset here) — relayed via MarkTechPost and OfficeChai coverage of the announcement. Artificial Analysis's own independent evaluation (artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-max and its per-benchmark leaderboards) measured GPQA Diamond 92.7 (close to Alibaba's claim) but Terminal-Bench v2.1 81.3 and HLE 41.4 — both notably below Alibaba's self-reported figures — so the AA-measured numbers are recorded here as the more independently verifiable source, with the discrepancy noted. Pricing ($2.00/$6.00 per 1M input/output tokens) is Alibaba Cloud Model Studio's Singapore/international rate; the China Beijing, Frankfurt, Virginia, Tokyo and Hong Kong regions price lower at $1.65/$4.951. Open weights, promised "next week" as of the Aug 3 announcement, arrived on 2026-08-13 — but as `qwen3-8-2-4t-a95b`, a reduced text-only variant with a 262K native window rather than this multimodal 1M-context Max build, which stays closed. Context window (983,616) and max output (131,072) match Alibaba Cloud Model Studio's official model-info page (context 1,000,000, max input 991,808 with 1,000,000 minus max-output overhead, max output 131,072); some coverage rounds context down to "1M tokens."

name: Qwen3.7 Max
strengths: Long-horizon autonomy — runs for tens of hours and thousands of tool calls without hand-holding
Precise instruction following, including multilingual and formatting constraints
Heavy caching discounts make repetitive agent loops cheap in practice
weaknesses: Very verbose — a real agentic session costs far more than the per-token rate suggests
Prose is over-engineered and reads machine-written
Closed weights, a break from the rest of the Qwen line
notes: SWE-bench Pro 60.6; Terminal-Bench 2.0 69.7. SWE-bench Verified 80.4 and HLE 41.4 lab/W&B-reported; MMLU-Pro 89.6 is third-party (LLM-Stats). Alibaba reports HMMT 97.1 instead of AIME.

name: Claude Opus 4.8
strengths: Flags its own uncertainty and asks rather than guessing — far less confident nonsense
The effort setting genuinely changes token spend, so quick and deep work share one model
More expressive and varied on creative work than the 4.x releases before it
weaknesses: The extra hedging is friction when you want a confident answer to a low-stakes question
Can get caught in self-correction loops, re-checking work that was already right
Clarifying questions interrupt fully autonomous runs that were meant to need no input
notes: HLE 49.8% no tools / 57.9% with tools. LMArena Elo corrected to 1484 (current Opus 4.8 Thinking listing, July 2026); an earlier 1510 figure did not match the live leaderboard. ARC-AGI-2 72.1% added July 2026 once ARC Prize published verified results: 72.08% at high effort (71.67% medium, 62.22% low).

name: Claude Fable 5
strengths: Holds decision quality steady across sessions that run for days, remembering why it chose something hours earlier
Plans in stages, delegates to sub-agents and checks its own work unprompted
Vision good enough to rebuild an interface from a screenshot
Acts rather than narrates — little time spent describing what it is about to do
weaknesses: Keeps working until something stops it, so agent loops need explicit stop rules or the cost runs away
Slow, and its depth of explanation is a cost when you wanted a quick scan
Token spend and latency swing enormously between low and max effort, making budgeting hard
notes: Shares weights with the restricted Claude Mythos 5 (vetted partners only). HLE 64.5% is with tools; GPQA/SWE figures are third-party — Anthropic retired saturated benchmarks from official reporting. Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.0% as reported in poolside's Laguna S 2.1 comparison table.

name: Gemma 4
strengths: Dense rather than sparse — predictable latency and memory, no routing variance to debug
Fits on a single high-end consumer GPU once quantized
Native system-role support and a switchable thinking mode, both unusual at this size
Reliable instruction following, which makes it a good retrieval and pipeline component
weaknesses: Full-precision serving still wants datacenter-class memory
No first-party hosted endpoint — you run it yourself or trust a third-party host
A component rather than an agent; it isn't built for long autonomous runs
notes: Benchmarks shown are for the 31B Dense variant. LMArena Elo (~1452) and the MMLU-Pro/GPQA/AIME/HLE figures are third-party community-reported, not an official Google table (BenchLM lists GPQA Diamond as 85.7% and HLE as 26.5%, so treat these as approximate). Pricing $0.10/$0.34 per MTok is OpenRouter's listing for google/gemma-4-31b-it — there is no first-party Google API price (Gemma 4 is not on Vertex AI), and other hosts differ (CoreWeave $0.12/$0.35, DeepInfra $0.13/$0.38 per Artificial Analysis). Weights were quietly published March 31, 2026; the formal Google blog announcement followed April 2, 2026. Knowledge cutoff (January 2025) confirmed via Google's official Gemma 4 model card (ai.google.dev).

name: GLM-5.2
strengths: Produces clean, production-ready code first time more often than its cost suggests
Reliable multi-turn tool calling — it doesn't lose track of what it already called
Unrestricted licence and mainstream inference-stack support make self-hosting straightforward
weaknesses: Very verbose — roughly double its predecessor's output per task, which shows up on both the bill and the clock
Noticeably slower per task than closed flagships of the same period
Text-only, so no screenshots, diagrams or PDFs
notes: SWE-bench Pro 62.1 reported; no SWE-bench Verified figure has been published. GPQA Diamond sources conflict (91.2 per the official Hugging Face model card vs ~80.3 in some third-party trackers) — official figure used. HLE 40.5% no tools / 54.7% with tools. Max output listed as 128K in most reporting; some sources cite up to 163,840 for extended reasoning. LMArena Elo 1469 is the "GLM-5.2 (max)" text-arena listing (arena.ai), the only GLM-5.2 variant on the board.

name: GPT-5.6 Sol
strengths: Stays on one task for days without drifting or declaring premature victory
Reaches the same answer in far fewer tokens than the model before it
Security work — threat modelling, code review, blue-teaming — is a deliberate specialism
weaknesses: Still verbose for interactive chat, despite being efficient on agentic work
Pre-deployment testing found it gaming its own evaluations, which makes any single score harder to trust
Priced well above its Terra and Luna siblings, which close much of the gap on everyday work
notes: The frontier tier of the three-model GPT-5.6 family (Sol / Terra / Luna), all released 2026-07-09. Context window and max output confirmed via OpenAI's developer docs. GPQA Diamond 94.6 and HLE 47.2 are OpenAI/Artificial Analysis-reported; MMLU-Pro 89.1 and ARC-AGI-2 92.5 (Max effort, per ARC Prize) are third-party. OpenAI published no SWE-bench or AIME figure for this family; SWE-bench Verified 96.2 is third-party, from Vals AI’s independent harness (leaderboard updated 2026-07-31, run at max reasoning effort), the same board that supplies Luna’s 93.0. AIME stays null. LMArena Elo 1485 is the "gpt-5.6-sol-xhigh" text-arena listing (arena.ai). Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 59. Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.8% from the GPT-5.6 launch comparison table (Sol 88.8 / Terra 87.4 / Luna 84.7). Sol's price held at $5.00/$30.00 through OpenAI's 2026-07-30 cuts to the other two tiers, which also added an optional fast mode: up to 2.5x the speed at twice the price.

name: GPT-5.6 Terra
strengths: Behaves like the flagship on ordinary work — the gap only opens on the hardest long-horizon agentic tasks
Long-context recall holds up close to Sol's, where the budget Luna tier falls away sharply
Full feature set rather than a cut-down one: image input, tool calling, extended reasoning, prompt caching and structured outputs
weaknesses: OpenAI published no per-tier academic benchmarks, so where it really sits against rivals is hard to pin down
Trails Sol most on exactly the long-horizon agentic work that justifies reaching for a frontier model
notes: Middle tier of the three-model GPT-5.6 family. OpenAI published only agentic suites per tier — Terminal-Bench 2.1 87.4%, Coding Agent Index 77.4, Agents' Last Exam 50.4, MRCR long-context recall 89.6% — and none of the site's tracked academic benchmarks, so those stay null. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 55 (vs Sol 59, Luna 51) at 140.4 output tokens/sec. Pricing is OpenAI's list rate, cut from $2.50/$15.00 to $2.00/$12.00 on 2026-07-30 (Luna was cut 80% in the same move). Context window per Artificial Analysis and OpenRouter; max output is tracker-reported, not from OpenAI's docs. Knowledge cutoff not published per tier.

name: GPT-5.6 Luna
strengths: Answers land almost immediately, so it works for interactive chat and not just overnight batch jobs
Holds its output format across thousands of calls — long structured-extraction runs come back parseable without repair passes
Carries the family's full toolkit rather than a cut-down one: image input, tool calling, prompt caching and tunable reasoning effort
weaknesses: Quietly switches from quoting sources to summarising them once a document set gets deep, so retrieval work needs chunking rather than one full-window prompt
Raising reasoning effort stops helping on genuinely unfamiliar problems — the top settings behave much like the low ones there
Character below the top effort settings is a different model in practice, which makes hands-on reports of it hard to reconcile
notes: Budget tier of the three-model GPT-5.6 family (Sol / Terra / Luna), all released 2026-07-09. Pricing is the post-cut rate: OpenAI cut Luna 80% from $1.00/$6.00 on 2026-07-30. Requests over 272K input tokens bill at 2x input and 1.5x output. Context window, max output and knowledge cutoff are from OpenAI's developer docs. GPQA Diamond 92.3 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 84.7 are from OpenAI's launch table, which also gave SWE-Bench Pro 62.7, Agents' Last Exam 50.3 and MRCR v2 long-context recall 41.3; HLE 37.2 (Artificial Analysis) and ARC-AGI-2 59.5 (ARC Prize) are max-effort figures, matching how Sol is recorded, and SWE-bench Verified 93.0 is third-party (Vals AI). Thinking Machines' Inkling-Small table, run at effort 0.99, reports Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.5 against OpenAI's 84.7 — official preferred — and its GPQA 89.5, HLE 35.6 and ARC-AGI-2 47.6 are the xhigh-effort variant rather than a conflict; its AIME 2026 97.6 is uncorroborated, so AIME stays null. LMArena Elo 1450 is the "gpt-5.6-luna-xhigh" text-arena listing. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 51 at max effort, 38 at the medium effort the costPerTask figure comes from.

name: Soofi S 30B-A3B
strengths: Throughput stays essentially flat as context grows, where dense-attention models slow down
German treated as a first-class language rather than a translation target
Few active parameters per token, so it runs quickly on modest hardware
Training data and process published in full, which matters for regulated deployments
weaknesses: An unaligned base checkpoint — no instruction tuning, no safety tuning, not usable as an assistant without fine-tuning
Licence terms were not final at release
A foundation to build on rather than a model that competes on capability
notes: No SWE-bench/AIME/HLE/LMArena/ARC-AGI-2 scores have been published; reported metrics instead cover HumanEval (73.8%), MBPP (70.2%, 84.2% for the German variant) and aggregate English/German scores. Coordinated by the KI Bundesverband and funded under Germany's IPCEI-CIS program; arXiv preprint posted 2026-07-10, press release and Hugging Face weights 2026-07-13. MMLU-Pro 51.4 and GPQA Diamond 43.4 corrected/added from the SOOFI consortium's own technical report (arXiv:2607.09424, Tables 4-5 and Figure 7), for the released base checkpoint iter_1056000 — not published in initial press coverage. The paper's Phase 3 training extends usable context to 1M tokens, but a separate long-context checkpoint is evaluated apart from the base-model benchmark table, so a single released context-window figure could not be confirmed.

name: Gemini 3.6 Flash
strengths: Sticks to the change you asked for instead of touching adjacent files during diagnostic work
Reaches the same result with fewer output tokens than the Flash before it
Available across Google's whole developer and enterprise surface on day one
weaknesses: Flash-tier depth ceiling — it executes well but doesn't crack genuinely hard reasoning
Arrived with no matching Pro-tier model in its generation, so there was nothing to escalate to
notes: Model card reports SWE-Bench Pro 58.7%, DeepSWE v1.1 49%, GDPval-AA v2 Elo 1421, and GDM-MRCR v2 91.8% at 128k; Google published none of the site's tracked benchmarks at launch. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 50 (third-party). GPQA Diamond 92.8% and HLE 38.3% are Artificial Analysis-measured, not Google-reported. LMArena Elo 1485 is the 'gemini-3.6-flash' text-arena listing (rank 12, arena.ai); it also sits #12 in the Frontend Code Arena at 1537. Announced 2026-07-21 alongside Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and the limited-access Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber.

name: Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite
strengths: Very high sustained token throughput — built for real-time, high-volume work
Holds a persona and multi-turn instructions far better than earlier Lite models
Drives a desktop and works over long inputs better than its size implies
weaknesses: Time to first token can feel unresponsive in chat even though it streams quickly once started
Small-model ceiling: it executes well but won't reason its way out of an unfamiliar problem
notes: Model card reports SWE-Bench Pro 54.2%, OSWorld-Verified 74.0%, MLE-Bench 39.2%, CharXiv 74.5% no tools / 76.5% with tools; Google published none of the tracked benchmark keys at launch. GPQA Diamond 83.8% and HLE 17.5% are Artificial Analysis-measured figures relayed by BenchLM — AA's own model page publishes only the composite Intelligence Index (36) — so treat both as third-party. LMArena Elo 1459 is the 'gemini-3.5-flash-lite' text-arena listing (rank 43, arena.ai). Also rolling out inside Google Search.

name: Claude Sonnet 5
strengths: Fast — responses land in seconds even with thinking enabled
Reads intent unusually well; it judges what you meant rather than what you literally typed
Steady enough on long agentic coding runs to be left running unattended
weaknesses: The most verbose Claude yet — it writes long even when told to be brief, and that length is where the cost goes
Personality divides users; some find it blunt or contrarian outside coding work
Deliberately weak at offensive security tasks
notes: Introductory pricing $2/$10 per MTok through Aug 31 2026, rising to standard $3/$15 on Sept 1. HLE 43.2% no tools / 57.4% with tools per Anthropic's system card. LMArena Elo 1461 is the 'Claude Sonnet 5 High' text-arena listing (arena.ai). SWE-bench Verified 85.2% is widely cited by third-party trackers (OpenRouter, Requesty, EdenAI), but Anthropic's own system card reports SWE-bench Pro (63.2%) instead — no official Verified figure confirmed. GPQA Diamond 91.1% is Artificial Analysis' own measurement (its gpqa-diamond leaderboard, relayed by BenchLM), not an Anthropic figure — a 96.2% number circulating on some trackers is unsourced and was rejected. ARC-AGI-2 and AIME remain unpublished: Anthropic did not report AIME for Sonnet 5 and ARC Prize has not tested it.

name: Grok 4.5
strengths: Finishes tasks in fewer steps, so agent runs are cheap in practice rather than just per token
Fast, decisive answers with very little hedging
Trained partly on real developer sessions, which shows in routine coding-agent work
weaknesses: Hallucinates far more than the model before it — confident, wrong, and in need of grounding for factual work
Drops off on the hardest and most novel problems, where 'close enough' isn't
Less public detail on safety and governance than rival labs published
notes: Announced July 8, public release July 9, 2026. GPQA Diamond 93.1%, HLE 40.3%, ARC-AGI-2 52.6%, and LMArena Elo 1468 are third-party (BenchLM/arena.ai) — xAI did not publish these itself, leading with SWE-bench Pro (64.7%) and SWE Marathon (29.0%) instead, so sweBench (Verified) is left null. Max output tokens unconfirmed — xAI's own model page documents the 500K context window and tiered pricing but no output cap; a ~30K figure appears only on secondary blogs, so left null. Knowledge cutoff confirmed as February 1, 2026 in xAI's official docs (docs.x.ai).

name: Muse Spark 1.1
strengths: Handles a multi-step browser task without hand-holding — tool and computer use are the point
Takes text, images, video, PDFs and audio in a single prompt
Good at creative and tone-shifting work: drafting, editing, adapting for an audience
weaknesses: Long-horizon agentic work still drifts where the leaders hold together
Closed and metered, a departure from Meta's open-weights history
notes: Second Meta Superintelligence Labs release, an upgrade to the original Muse Spark (April 2026) and Meta's first paid API model. HLE 62.1% (with tools) per Meta/BenchLM; Artificial Analysis separately reports a 40% → 45% no-tools HLE gain over the original Muse Spark. SWE-bench Pro 61.5% reported; no SWE-bench Verified figure published. GPQA Diamond 89.8% and LMArena Elo 1495 ('Muse Spark 1.1' text-arena listing, arena.ai) are third-party. ARC-AGI-2, MMLU-Pro, and AIME not published for this release. Knowledge cutoff not disclosed.

name: Claude Opus 5
strengths: Verifies its own work unprompted, delegates readily, and will widen a task's scope on its own judgement
Holds the thread across long multi-step work and pins down vague requirements before building
Reads a large unfamiliar codebase carefully before it changes anything
Solves novel-pattern problems that no earlier model could, rather than recalling them
weaknesses: Verbose and pushy — it narrates constantly, and default output length responds to prompting more than to the effort setting
Early users describe it as neurotic and apologetic, and less willing to follow a prescribed workflow than Opus 4.8
Easy to misconfigure: effort and skill settings change its behavior more than the version bump does
notes: HLE 56.3% no tools / 64.7% with tools. SWE-bench Verified 96.0% is Anthropic's own system-card figure (five-trial average); a third-party aggregator (vals.ai) cites 97.0%. GPQA Diamond varies 93.4-93.7% across trackers; 93.7% used. ARC-AGI-2 90.4% (max effort) and ARC-AGI-3 30.2% (high effort, a separate untracked scale) per ARC Prize (arcprize.org). Max output is 128K on the synchronous API, up to 300K via the Message Batches API. AIME not published — Anthropic appears to be moving to newer evals (IMO 2026, Frontier-Bench v0.1) instead.

name: Inkling
strengths: Built to be fine-tuned — same-day tuning support and an unrestricted licence
Takes images and long audio natively, still unusual for an open-weights model
Open at frontier scale from a US lab, with no regional restrictions
weaknesses: Weak factuality — it hallucinates at a high rate and needs grounding for anything factual
Degrades in long multi-turn conversations
Positioned as a base to customise, not a model to deploy as it ships
notes: Thinking Machines Lab's first production model, released 2026-07-15. All benchmarks are the lab's own model-card figures at effort=0.99; HLE is 29.7% text-only / 46.0% with tools, and the model card reports Global-MMLU-Lite 88.7% rather than MMLU-Pro, so MMLU-Pro, LMArena Elo and ARC-AGI-2 are left null. Pricing is Tinker's 64K-context tier under a limited-time 50% discount ($1.87/$4.68 per MTok, $0.374 cached); the 256K tier is $3.74/$9.36, and OpenRouter hosts list about $1.00/$4.05. Context is 1M with the open weights but capped at 256K on the Tinker API; no max output figure is published. Also reported: SWE-Bench Pro Public 54.3%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 63.8%, GDPval-AA v2 Elo 1238, MMMU Pro 73.5%. ARC-AGI-2 36.5% (and ARC-AGI-1 79.5%) and LMArena Elo 1441 were added later, from the Inkling-Small comparison table and the LMArena text leaderboard respectively.

name: Laguna S 2.1
strengths: Trained to keep checking its work and retry failed approaches instead of giving up mid-run
Small enough to serve on a single workstation-class box while doing long-horizon coding
Full evaluation trajectories published, so its behavior can be inspected rather than taken on trust
Licence permits commercial use and modification
weaknesses: A coding specialist — text-only, and it was neither built nor measured for knowledge, maths or general reasoning
Emits invalid JSON on nested tool calls inside some third-party agent scaffolds
Tuned closely to its own harness; behavior shifts when moved to a different agent framework
notes: Terminal-Bench 2.1 is the only tracked benchmark reported: poolside published agentic coding evals only, all with thinking enabled — Terminal-Bench 2.1 70.2%, SWE-bench Multilingual 78.5%, SWE-Bench Pro public 59.4%, DeepSWE v1.1 40.4%, SWE Atlas 46.2%, Toolathlon Verified 49.7% (pass@1 over 3-4 attempts). Without thinking, Terminal-Bench 2.1 drops to 60.4% and DeepSWE to 16.5%. SWE-bench Verified is absent from poolside's blog and Hugging Face model card — the Multilingual and Pro figures are different splits and are not recorded as a Verified score. Pricing is the OpenRouter listing served by poolside ($0.10/$0.20 per MTok, $0.01 cached read); poolside publishes no separate per-token price sheet and also offers a free 256K-context tier. Knowledge cutoff of November 2025 is poolside's own, stated in the launch post while ruling out contamination on an Erdős-problem result; the model shares XS 2.1's pre-training data. Max output 131,072 tokens per the OpenRouter endpoint spec. Artificial Analysis does not cover poolside models, so there is no cost-per-task figure.

name: Nemotron 3 Super
strengths: Among the fastest open models at its capability — roughly 450 output tokens/sec on hosted endpoints
Activates about a tenth of its parameters per token, so it serves far cheaper than its size implies
Handles very long inputs without the slowdown dense models hit, thanks to the hybrid state-space design
weaknesses: Text-only, so no screenshots, diagrams or PDFs
Reasoning depth well short of frontier flagships — a fast workhorse rather than a hard-problem model
notes: Middle of the Nemotron 3 family; 120B total / 12.7B active MoE. MMLU-Pro 83.73, SWE-bench Verified 60.47, AIME 2025 90.21 and HLE 18.26 per llm-stats' launch analysis. GPQA Diamond left null deliberately: the reported 79.23 is labelled "GPQA no tools", which NVIDIA's own report treats as distinct from GPQA Diamond. Pricing is DeepInfra's rate; OpenRouter lists $0.085/$0.40 and the cross-provider median is about $0.30/$0.80. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 36.0.

name: Nemotron 3 Ultra
strengths: Hybrid Mamba-Transformer routing holds throughput up as context grows, where dense attention models slow down
Serves faster than most open models near its size — over 400 tokens/sec on hosted endpoints
Ships training data and recipes alongside the weights, so it can be genuinely retrained rather than only run
Licence permits commercial deployment and self-hosting without negotiation
weaknesses: Text-only — no images, screenshots or documents
Trails the leading Chinese open-weights models on composite intelligence despite its size
NVIDIA published no standard academic benchmark table at launch, so it is hard to place precisely
notes: Largest of the three-model Nemotron 3 family (Nano, Super, Ultra); 550B total / 55B active MoE. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 47.7 — ahead of Gemma 4 31B (39.2) and Nemotron 3 Super (36.0), behind Kimi K2.6 (53.9). None of the site's tracked benchmarks could be attributed with confidence: NVIDIA's technical report contains many ablation and quantisation tables rather than a single headline model table, so they stay null rather than risk quoting an intermediate checkpoint. Pricing is OpenRouter's listing; NVIDIA publishes no first-party per-token price. Context is 1M per NVIDIA, though OpenRouter serves a 512K effective window.

name: Hy3
strengths: Tool calls hold their shape across third-party agent scaffoldings instead of needing harness-specific patches
Recovers from a failed tool call rather than looping on it — the reliability bug Tencent set out to fix after the preview
Reasoning is a per-request switch, so quick answers and deep work come off one endpoint
Apache 2.0 with no regional carve-outs, unlike the Hunyuan releases before it
weaknesses: Answers confidently where it should abstain — third-party knowledge probes catch it fabricating far more often than Tencent's own hallucination figures suggest
Text-only: no images, screenshots or documents
Thinks at length on high effort, so agentic runs consume far more output budget than the token price implies
notes: Successor to April's Hy3 Preview; the licence moved to Apache 2.0 with this release. GPQA Diamond 90.4, SWE-bench Verified 78.0 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 71.7 are Tencent's own figures, published as an image and transcribed by launch coverage — Artificial Analysis independently measures GPQA 89.7 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 64.4. HLE 31.6% is Artificial Analysis' no-tools run; Tencent reports 53.2% with tools. Also reported: SWE-bench Pro 57.9%, SWE-bench Multilingual 75.8%, DeepSWE 28.0%, and a blind 270-expert evaluation at 2.67/4. MMLU-Pro, AIME and ARC-AGI-2 were not published. Pricing is the OpenRouter listing — Tencent publishes no first-party per-token price sheet.

name: LongCat-2.0
strengths: Trained and served end to end on domestic Chinese accelerators, with no Nvidia silicon anywhere in the loop
Spent two months at the top of OpenRouter as the anonymous 'Owl Alpha' before anyone knew whose it was — the reception came before the branding
Careful and thorough on review-style work where you want it to explain what it found
MIT-licensed at trillion-parameter scale, with a clean commercial grant
weaknesses: Verbose and slow enough to be awkward for conversational pairing — it suits long unattended runs better
Hands-on comparisons put its generated apps a generation behind GLM 5.2's: rougher and buggier despite benchmark parity
Fabricates readily on factual questions, and knowledge coverage lags its agentic ability badly
notes: Announced 2026-06-29 on GitHub, Hugging Face and Meituan's own platform (some coverage dates it 2026-06-30); it had been running anonymously on OpenRouter as 'Owl Alpha' for roughly two months beforehand. GPQA Diamond 88.9 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 70.8 are Meituan's in-house harness figures — Artificial Analysis independently measures 78.0 and 50.2 on the same two benchmarks, and HLE 32.1% is Artificial Analysis' no-tools run since Meituan published none. Also reported: SWE-bench Pro 59.5%, SWE-bench Multilingual 77.3%, FORTE 73.2%, BrowseComp 79.9%; no SWE-bench Verified, MMLU-Pro, AIME or ARC-AGI-2 figure exists. Pricing is LongCat's standard API rate, with a launch promotion at $0.30/$1.20. Max output is the OpenRouter endpoint spec; some coverage cites 131,072. Meituan says only 'AI ASIC superpods' — the widely repeated 50,000 Huawei Ascend 910C figure comes from Chinese media, not from Meituan.

name: Motif-3-Beta
strengths: A from-scratch architecture rather than a re-parameterised open model — its grouped differential latent attention learns a per-group noise head and subtracts it back out
Carries a multi-token-prediction head, so it self-speculates without a separate draft model
Korean is a first-class training target, not a translation afterthought
Weights are ungated — no access request, no waitlist
weaknesses: An explicitly intermediate checkpoint with the final Motif-3 still to come, so its behavior is a moving target
Non-commercial licence only, a step back from Motif-2's Apache terms, which rules it out of production
Custom modelling code needs trust_remote_code and a vendor vLLM image tested only on B200 and H200 — anything else is on you
notes: Preview checkpoint from Motif Technologies, a ~30-person Moreh subsidiary building under South Korea's sovereign-AI programme; weights landed on Hugging Face 2026-07-20 and Artificial Analysis dates the checkpoint 2026-07-14. Motif publishes no benchmark table of its own beyond an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index of 44, so GPQA Diamond 86.9, Terminal-Bench 2.1 70.8 and HLE 38.2 here are Artificial Analysis' own measurements; MMLU-Pro, SWE-bench, AIME, LMArena and ARC-AGI-2 are unpublished. No per-token price exists and no aggregator serves it, so cost per task is unset — the only hosted route is a free chat at chat.motiftech.io, hence availability 'restricted' despite downloadable weights.

name: Laguna XS 2.1
strengths: Fits on a 36 GB Mac, so a long-horizon coding agent can stay entirely local
Thinks between tool calls and lets you switch that off per request
Ships FP8, NVFP4 and INT4 checkpoints alongside BF16, plus speculator models that roughly double achieved tokens/sec
Licence permits commercial use and modification
weaknesses: A coding specialist — text-only, and neither built nor measured for knowledge, maths or general reasoning
Ollama on Apple Silicon can return empty output, a Metal overflow in the MoE down-projection with the fix still pending
Evaluated only in poolside's own harness with thinking on, so behavior in other agent frameworks is unmeasured
notes: Smaller sibling of Laguna S 2.1, released three weeks earlier; it replaced Laguna XS.2, which poolside sunset on its API a week after launch. SWE-bench Verified 70.9% is poolside's own figure, mean pass@1 over four attempts with thinking enabled; also reported are SWE-bench Multilingual 63.1%, SWE-Bench Pro public 47.6% and Terminal-Bench 2.0 37.5% — the 2.0 score is not comparable to the 2.1 figures tracked here, so terminalBench stays null. Pricing is poolside's list rate; OpenRouter was serving it at a 40% discount and also offers a free tier. No MMLU-Pro, GPQA, AIME, HLE, LMArena or ARC-AGI-2 score has been published, and knowledge cutoff is undisclosed.

name: Inkling-Small
strengths: Thinking effort sweeps from minimal to xhigh, and the whole performance curve sits above its much larger sibling's
Reads audio and images through the same encoder-free stack, and will drive Python to crop and zoom into a chart it cannot read directly
Overtook the full-size Inkling on reasoning and agentic coding after two extra weeks of RL on a distilled checkpoint
Runs cleanly across third-party coding and agent harnesses, not just its own
weaknesses: Factually thin — it covers less ground than Inkling and still needs retrieval and human review for anything consequential
Degrades in long multi-turn conversations, and the model card concedes it sometimes ignores instructions outright
Multi-step tool use went backwards versus Inkling even as the reasoning scores went up
notes: Thinking Machines Lab's second release, a 276B/12B MoE trained on GB300 systems. All benchmarks are the lab's own model-card figures at effort 0.99; SWE-bench Verified uses a bash-only harness and Terminal-Bench 2.1 an internal one with web-contaminated solutions scored zero. HLE 31.6% is text-only no tools / 47.8% with tools. MMLU-Pro is not reported (Global-MMLU-Lite 86.7% instead). Also reported: SWE-bench Pro public 55.9%, GDPval-AA v2 Elo 1269, MMMU Pro 74.0%, IFBench 82.2%, ARC-AGI-1 84.0%. Context is 1M with the open weights but OpenRouter serves 512K; Thinking Machines publishes only the $1.20 output price, and $0.50 input is the OpenRouter listing (Artificial Analysis lists $0.30). LMArena Elo 1431 is an AutoEval rating.

name: Qwen3.7 Flash
strengths: Takes video as well as images — the only model in the Qwen3.7 line that does
Thinking is switchable rather than always-on, with a large dedicated thinking budget
Cheap enough at the base tier to run as a subagent you never bother metering
weaknesses: Latency has a long tail — the slowest percentile runs to well over a minute, which cascades through tool-calling chains
Roughly one tool call in eleven comes back malformed, worse than the Plus tier in the same family
Transcribes text out of images poorly, so document and screenshot work needs a different model
notes: Announced only as a one-paragraph QwenCloud changelog entry on 2026-07-25, with no technical report, no benchmark table and no parameter count; the OpenRouter listing went live 2026-07-27 under a snapshot named qwen3.7-flash-2026-07-15. None of the site's tracked benchmarks has been published or independently measured — neither Artificial Analysis nor LMArena has run it, so cost per task is unset. Pricing is the sub-32K prompt tier; 32K-256K prompts cost $0.10/$0.40 and 256K-1M cost $0.20/$0.80. Usable input caps at 991,808 tokens in standard mode. Fine-tuning is unsupported and batch inference is Beijing-region only.

name: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
strengths: Same weights and architecture as the April preview — every gain comes from a rebuilt post-training recipe, not new pre-training
Clears DeepSeek's own larger V4-Pro preview on every agentic benchmark the lab published
Three reasoning-effort levels and a speculative-decoding module carried inside the one checkpoint
MIT-licensed and ungated, so on-premise commercial deployment needs no negotiation
weaknesses: Thinks at length before acting on max effort — long agent runs burn far more tokens and wall-clock than the per-call latency suggests
Fabricates heavily on knowledge probes, and factual coverage has not moved with the agentic gains
Ships without a Jinja chat template — messages go through DeepSeek's own Python encoding scripts instead
notes: The production release of DeepSeek-V4-Flash, superseding April's preview: same 284B/13B MoE and DSpark speculative-decoding module, with all gains from re-post-training. Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.7 is DeepSeek's own figure at max reasoning effort in its minimal-mode harness; Artificial Analysis measures 78.7 on the same benchmark. GPQA Diamond 90.8 and HLE 36.8% (no tools) are Artificial Analysis' measurements — DeepSeek published neither. Also reported by DeepSeek: NL2Repo 54.2, Cybergym 76.7, DeepSWE 54.4, Toolathlon-Verified 70.3, Agents' Last Exam 25.2. MMLU-Pro, SWE-bench Verified, AIME, LMArena and ARC-AGI-2 are unpublished. Artificial Analysis scores it 50 on its Intelligence Index, 10 points above the April preview’s 40. Max output is the 384K DeepSeek recommends for high and max effort; the OpenRouter endpoint caps completions at 65,536.

name: Claude Sonnet 4.6
strengths: Declares agentic tasks finished far less often when they aren't — false claims of task completion dropped noticeably from Sonnet 4.5
Holds up across the full 1M-token window rather than degrading well before the limit
Drives a desktop reliably enough for real office workflows — Anthropic reports Opus-class results on tasks that previously needed the bigger model
weaknesses: Terser and more emotionally flat in casual conversation than Sonnet 4.5 — reads as dry and abbreviated unless prompted otherwise
Takes unusually assertive initiative in agentic coding and turns ruthless when a system prompt tells it to optimize single-mindedly for an objective — needs explicit guardrails
Still trails top human performance on computer-use tasks; Anthropic continues to point to Opus 4.6 for the deepest reasoning work
notes: SWE-bench Verified 79.6% is the system card's 10-trial average (adaptive thinking, max effort); a specific prompt modification pushed it to 80.2%. Terminal-Bench 2.0 59.1% (default thinking) is not comparable to 2.1 scores elsewhere, so the terminalBench field is left null. ARC-AGI-2 60.4% is ARC Prize Foundation's own reported figure (120k thinking tokens, high effort); Anthropic's internal reproduction reports 58.3% (ARC-AGI-2 Verified). HLE 33.2% no tools / 49.0% with tools. AIME 95.6% (no tools) — Anthropic flags possible dataset contamination as a reason the score may be inflated. Max output is 128K per Anthropic's own models table; AWS Bedrock's model card lists 64K for the same model — Anthropic's own figure is used here.

name: Mach-1 Additive 35B
strengths: Runs entirely offline on a single 16GB+ Apple Silicon Mac, or streamed straight into a browser tab via WebGPU — no account, API key, or cloud dependency
Compresses to roughly a tenth the footprint of its teacher through an additive, multiplication-free inference scheme at 1.7 bits per weight
Reached that compression with under 15 GPU-hours of retraining, far less than comparable extreme-quantization approaches
weaknesses: Debut release from a three-person team with no coverage yet on LMArena, Artificial Analysis, or any independent benchmark leaderboard — real-world behavior outside the vendor's own figures is unverified
Instruction-following degraded more than reasoning or math under compression in the vendor's own retention testing, the softest spot in an otherwise strong profile
No hosted API at launch — obtaining it means downloading multi-gigabyte weights or running the in-browser demo, not a quick sign-up
notes: Company and model both launched 2026-08-02/03; benchmark figures Syzygy has published are self-reported retention percentages against its teacher model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) across 12 evals (e.g. AIME26 99.5%, MATH-500 99.4%, IFBench 83.2% retention), not absolute scores on this site's tracked benchmarks, so all eight benchmark fields are left null. License (Apache-2.0) is inherited unmodified from the Qwen base weights (copyright notice in the repo's LICENSE file still reads Alibaba Cloud). Syzygy's own figures claim up to 120 output tokens/sec on consumer hardware; left out of the speed field since Artificial Analysis has not measured it.

name: Ling-2.6-1T
strengths: Skips multi-step chain-of-thought in favor of a "fast thinking" mode, giving high-quality answers at roughly a quarter the token cost of comparable reasoning models
Hybrid MLA/linear-attention architecture keeps latency and VRAM use down at the full 256K context length
Open weights under a permissive licence, with drop-in compatibility for existing agent scaffolds (Claude Code, OpenCode, and others)
weaknesses: A non-reasoning model by design — not built for deep multi-step reasoning tasks, where its Ring-2.6 thinking sibling is the intended tool instead
Humanity's Last Exam score is low relative to its coding and agentic numbers, consistent with a model tuned for execution over broad expert knowledge
Too new for independent coverage on LMArena or Artificial Analysis' full benchmark suite at launch
notes: Ant Group's Bailing team announced Ling-2.6-1T on 2026-04-24 (weights open-sourced 2026-04-30 on Hugging Face/ModelScope); Maia's supplied link (ling-1t.ai/ling-2-6-1t) is not an official Ant Group/InclusionAI domain and was not used as a source. GPQA Diamond, HLE and AIME26 figures are third-party aggregator reports (aiflashreport.com, howaiworks.ai), not confirmed on an official Ant Group table or on Artificial Analysis directly — treat as secondary-sourced. Pricing is Artificial Analysis' median across API providers ($0.30/$2.50 per MTok); OpenRouter separately lists a lower $0.075/$0.625 rate, which may be promotional. Context window is 262,144 tokens via the public API; some coverage cites a 1M-token native/trained context. Total/active parameters are reported as roughly 1.03T/63B (MoE).

name: gpt-oss-120b
strengths: Fits on a single 80GB datacenter GPU at native precision, so it's a genuinely self-hostable release rather than a paper-only open weights drop
Reasoning effort is a plain system-prompt string (low/medium/high), trading latency for depth without swapping checkpoints
Exposes its full chain-of-thought in the output rather than summarizing or hiding it, unlike OpenAI's closed reasoning models
weaknesses: Hallucinates markedly more than OpenAI's closed models on people and fact lookups — the expected trade-off of a smaller open weight store of world knowledge
Locked to OpenAI's bespoke Harmony response format; feeding it a generic chat template silently breaks tool calls and reasoning
Inherited safety training leans toward refusal, and self-hosters report it overcorrecting on benign prompts
notes: OpenAI's first open-weight release since GPT-2. GPQA Diamond 80.1%, HLE 14.9% and AIME 2025 92.5% are no-tools scores at high reasoning effort per OpenAI's model card (arXiv:2508.10925); with tools, GPQA rises to 80.9%, HLE to 19.0%, AIME to 97.9%. MMLU-Pro 80.8 is from the official Hugging Face model card. Terminal-Bench reported is 2.0 (18.7%), not the tracked 2.1 metric, so left null here. Pricing ($0.03/$0.17 per MTok) is a representative third-party hosted rate (OpenRouter/CoreWeave) — OpenAI's own API docs list the model with no attached price, and rates vary roughly 9x across hosts (e.g. AWS Bedrock charges $0.15/$0.60).

name: gpt-oss-20b
strengths: Runs in about 16GB of memory, putting it within reach of a single consumer GPU or a high-end laptop
Competition math performance keeps pace with its 120B sibling despite the much smaller footprint
Same effort-string reasoning control and exposed chain-of-thought as the 120B model
weaknesses: Hallucinates even more than the 120B on people and fact lookups, the cost of a smaller knowledge store
Also requires the Harmony response format — a generic chat template silently breaks tool calls
Agentic terminal/tool-use tasks lag well behind its math and coding strength — a narrow specialist rather than an all-rounder
notes: Released alongside gpt-oss-120b as the lower-latency, edge-deployable sibling. GPQA Diamond 71.5%, HLE 10.9% and AIME 2025 91.7% are no-tools scores at high reasoning effort per OpenAI's model card (arXiv:2508.10925); with tools, GPQA rises to 74.2%, HLE to 17.3%, AIME to 98.7% (edging past the 120B model). MMLU-Pro 73.6 is from the official Hugging Face model card. Terminal-Bench reported is 2.0 (roughly 3%, sources conflict between 3.1% and 3.4%), not the tracked 2.1 metric, so left null here. Pricing ($0.03/$0.13 per MTok) is a representative third-party hosted rate (OpenRouter) — OpenAI's own API docs list the model with no attached price, and rates vary across hosts (e.g. AWS Bedrock charges $0.07/$0.30).

name: MiniMax-M2
strengths: Interleaved thinking alternates plan, act and reflect within a single response rather than reasoning once and executing blind — makes long, tool-heavy agent loops easier to debug
Genuinely fast for its price bracket — MiniMax reports roughly double the throughput of Claude Sonnet at a small fraction of the cost
Sparse MoE with only 10B active parameters keeps latency low on long agentic sessions despite the 230B total size
weaknesses: Programming ability trails the leading closed models, competitive mainly against other open-weight coding models
Reliable tool use depends on the interleaved-thinking output format; wrapping it in a non-standard harness reportedly degrades results
As the first release in a fast-iterating series, MiniMax had already shipped two further point updates within four months
notes: Officially announced 2025-10-27 (minimax.io/news/minimax-m2). Hugging Face model card lists 230B total / 10B active parameters. GPQA-Diamond 78, AIME25 78, HLE 12.5% (without tools, 31.8% with), MMLU-Pro 82 and SWE-bench Verified 69.4 are from the official Hugging Face README. A 46.3 'Terminal-Bench' figure also appears there without a version label, so left null here rather than assume 2.1. Context window 204,800 tokens per MiniMax's own API docs; max output isn't stated in MiniMax's docs (a third-party 131,072 figure was not independently corroborated, so left null). Licensed under MiniMax's 'Modified MIT' terms: commercial use is unrestricted, with an in-product attribution requirement triggered only above 100M monthly active users or $30M annual revenue.

name: MiniMax-M2.5
strengths: SWE-bench Verified jumped sharply over M2 in under four months, the fastest capability gain in the series so far
Cheap enough to run continuously — MiniMax markets a roughly $1/hour cost at 100 output tokens/sec
A separate 'Lightning' throughput mode trades some cost efficiency for materially faster output when latency matters more than price
weaknesses: Still text-only and capped at the same ~205K context as M2 — the long-context and multimodal jump waited for M3
MMLU-Pro wasn't part of MiniMax's own benchmark table at launch, an unusual omission next to its detailed coding and agentic suite
Superseded within four months by M3, the usual pace for this series
notes: Officially announced 2026-02-12 (minimax.io/news/minimax-m25); MiniMax's own release material frames this as an iteration on M2/M2.1 rather than an explicit replacement of either, so predecessorId is left null. GPQA-Diamond 85.2, AIME25 86.3 and HLE 19.4% (without tools) are from the official Hugging Face README's comparison table; SWE-bench Verified 80.2%, which MiniMax describes as a new record for the series, is from the same announcement. MMLU-Pro is absent from MiniMax's own table; a third-party 74% figure (oddly lower than M2's official 82) could not be corroborated and looks inconsistent with M2.5's gains elsewhere, so left null. Context window confirmed at 204,800 tokens via MiniMax's own API docs — the same as M2; the 1M-token window is M3-only, despite some third-party trackers conflating the two. Pricing shown is the standard (non-Lightning) tier; the Lightning variant runs faster (100 tok/s vs 50) at roughly double the output price ($0.30/$2.40 vs $0.15/$1.20).

name: MiniMax-M3
strengths: First open-weight model from any lab to combine a 1M-token context window, frontier-tier coding, and native image/video understanding in one checkpoint
New MiniMax Sparse Attention architecture gives large prefill/decode speedups over M2 at long context, so the 1M window is reportedly usable rather than nominal
Can drive a desktop computer-use agent (MiniMax Code) directly, not just chat
weaknesses: License tightened from M2's largely unrestricted terms to a revenue-gated community license requiring authorization above $20M annual revenue
Multimodal input is new to this generation, so image/video handling is comparatively less battle-tested than its text/coding path
Early hands-on reception is cautiously optimistic rather than settled — reliability on production agent loops still needs workload-specific testing
notes: Officially announced 2026-06-01 (minimax.io/blog/minimax-m3); some third-party trackers (e.g. OpenRouter) list 2026-05-31, likely the weights-availability date. Total/active parameters ~428B/23B per the Hugging Face model card. SWE-bench Verified 80.5% and Terminal-Bench 2.1 66.0% are corroborated across the Hugging Face README and MiniMax's own blog. GPQA Diamond, AIME, HLE, MMLU-Pro and ARC-AGI-2 were not extractable — MiniMax's benchmark table at launch is an embedded image rather than machine-readable text, and no independent source reproduced these specific figures. Licensed under the bespoke 'MiniMax Community License': free for non-commercial use; commercial use under $20M annual revenue requires only a notice email and a 'Built with MiniMax' attribution label, above that threshold prior written authorization is required. Third-party framing calls M3 a 'successor to M2.7' (not tracked here), but MiniMax's own material explicitly keeps M2.5 available as a cheaper option for some workloads rather than deprecating it, so predecessorId is left null. Pricing is the standard tier for inputs up to 512K tokens; above that the rate doubles to $0.60/$2.40 per MTok.

name: Seed 2.0 Pro
strengths: Ranked in the top handful of models on human-preference arena testing at launch, reflecting strong everyday conversational quality rather than just benchmark strength
Handles long, multi-part Chinese-language instructions — tone control, formatting, few-shot pattern-following — noticeably better than its Seed1.8 predecessor
Native video tool-use (VideoCut) lets it re-inspect footage at a higher frame rate mid-task instead of reasoning over static frames alone
weaknesses: ByteDance's own report is unusually candid about real gaps against Claude on repository-scale coding and against Gemini on long-tail factual knowledge
Long-context retrieval (needle-style) tasks lag its overall reasoning strength — it can lose track of scattered details in very long inputs
Hallucination-robustness trails GPT-5.2 on several factuality checks despite leading on many other evaluations
notes: Officially launched 2026-02-14 (Seed2.0 Model Card, ByteDance Seed, hosted at lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com; announcement blog at seed.bytedance.com). MMLU-Pro 87.0, GPQA Diamond 88.9, AIME 2025 98.3 and HLE 32.4% (no-tools, text-only) are from the model card's Table 3; SWE-bench Verified 76.5% is from Table 11 (agentic capacity evaluation); ARC-AGI-2 37.5 is from Table 3's General Reasoning section. Terminal-Bench figure in the same table (55.8) is version 2.0, not the tracked 2.1 metric, so left null here. LMArena listed only a rank (6th on the Text Arena leaderboard as of 2026-02-16), not an Elo score, so lmarenaElo stays null. Context window (256K) and max output (128K) are corroborated across third-party trackers (CloudPrice, others) citing the API model id 'doubao-seed-2-0-pro-260215'; not independently confirmed on an official ByteDance spec page, so treat as secondary-sourced. Pricing from the model card's Table 1 ($0.47/$2.37 per MTok, quoted alongside ¥3.41/¥17.04).

name: Seed 2.1 Pro
strengths: ByteDance's launch framing shifts from Seed 2.0's broad multimodal upgrade to a narrower, workflow-oriented bar: whether the model can carry one real task from requirement to validated result
A preview build placed level with Claude Opus 4.6 on the Code Arena frontend leaderboard within days of release
Ships as a paired Pro/Turbo lineup from day one, so a lower-cost, lower-latency sibling is available immediately rather than following months later
weaknesses: No model card or benchmark table has been published at launch — every capability claim so far is qualitative ('leading', 'comparable to GPT-5.5') rather than a disclosed number
Parameter counts and knowledge cutoff remain undisclosed, unlike the detailed technical report ByteDance published for Seed 2.0
Too new for independent benchmark or arena coverage beyond a single preview-build leaderboard placement
notes: Officially launched 2026-06-23 at Volcano Engine's FORCE conference (seed.bytedance.com/en/blog/seed2-1-officially-released-advancing-ai-productivity); ByteDance's own post makes only qualitative claims (leads Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-Bench Pro, SciCode, OSWorld, MobileWorld, MMMU-Pro among named benchmarks) without publishing a benchmark table or model card, unlike Seed 2.0 — so all eight tracked benchmark fields are left null rather than guessed from prose. A Seed 2.1 Pro preview build ranked 8th on arena.ai's Code Arena frontend leaderboard with a score of 1539, level with Claude Opus 4.6, but that is a different (frontend-coding) leaderboard from the tracked overall text lmarenaElo, so left null here too. Context window (256K) is corroborated across multiple third-party API trackers citing Volcano Engine's model list; max output could not be pinned to a reliable single figure and is left null. Pricing (¥6/¥30 per MTok ≈ $0.83/$4.14) is from ByteDance's own announcement; Seed 2.1 Turbo is priced at half the Pro rate.

name: ERNIE 5.0
strengths: First Chinese model to break the LMArena Text global top 10 at launch, on par with GPT-5.1 High and ahead of Gemini 2.5 Pro at the time
Native full-modal (text/image/audio/video) unified modeling rather than a bolted-on vision encoder — leads on document- and chart-understanding benchmarks like OCRBench, DocVQA and ChartQA
Trillion-parameter MoE activates under 3% of parameters per inference, keeping serving cost down despite the 2.4T total size
weaknesses: Real-world testing found it ignoring explicit format instructions (e.g. firing the image generator when told to output SVG code only), pointing to instruction-following gaps behind its benchmark scores
Developers reported tool-call loops and rough edges running it in agentic workflows despite strong raw capability
Baidu discloses no knowledge-cutoff date
notes: Officially launched 2026-01-22 at the Ernie Moment Conference 2026 Shanghai (a preview build, ERNIE-5.0-Preview, had circulated from November 2025). Benchmark figures (MMLU-Pro 83.80, GPQA-Diamond 86.36, AIME 2025 89.06, HLE 25.81) are Baidu's own post-trained-model numbers from the ERNIE 5.0 Technical Report (arxiv.org/abs/2602.04705, Table in the post-training results section) — self-reported and not independently reproduced; the same report separately lists lower base-model-only scores (MMLU-Pro 75.58, GPQA-Diamond 57.30) which are not used here. lmarenaElo 1447 is the official arena.ai Text leaderboard score for the ERNIE-5.0-0110 checkpoint (independent measurement, preferred over Baidu's own '#8 globally / 1460' launch-day figure, which the leaderboard has since revised). SWE-bench Verified and ARC-AGI-2 were not reported by Baidu or found on any independent leaderboard. Pricing ($0.60/$2.10 per MTok) and context/output figures (128K/65,536) are corroborated across third-party trackers citing Baidu Qianfan's console, not confirmed on an official Baidu pricing page directly. Closed weights; no license record.

name: ERNIE 5.1
strengths: Claimed #1 Chinese model on both the LMArena Text and Search leaderboards at launch, reaching #4 globally on Search

Reaches ERNIE 5.0-beating benchmark results while training at roughly 6% of the pre-training compute of comparable frontier models, by extracting the strongest sub-network from ERNIE 5.0's elastic sub-model matrix rather than training from scratch
Agentic evaluation (tau-cubed-bench, SpreadsheetBench-Verified) reported ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Pro; math accuracy (AIME26 with tools) among the highest reported of any model
weaknesses: Trails GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 on MMLU-Pro broad-knowledge testing despite leading on math and agentic evaluations
Text-only — dropped ERNIE 5.0's native image/audio/video input, so multimodal work still requires pairing it with another model
Developers flagged tool-call loops and rough edges in agentic workflows at launch, echoing ERNIE 5.0's production reliability complaints
notes: Officially released 2026-05-08 (ernie.baidu.com/blog/posts/ernie-5.1-0508-release), with wider rollout at the Create 2026 developer conference May 13-14.
